claim: Nearly 30% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDACs) exhibit a marked overexpression of monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1).
source: Nearly 30% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDACs) exhibit a marked overexpression of monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) offering a unique opportunity for therapy.
evidence: Based on comparison of RNAseq datasets from TCGA and CCLE with GTEx portal, and immunohistochemistry on tissue microarrays showing 56% of 95 PDACs were positive for MCT1.

claim: Biochemical inhibitors of MCT1 have proven unsuccessful in clinical trials.
source: However, biochemical inhibitors of MCT1 have proven unsuccessful in clinical trials.
evidence: References to AZD3965 not being effective in treatment of solid tumors.

claim: 3BP is a cytotoxic agent that is known to be transported into cells via MCT1.
source: 3BP is a cytotoxic agent that is known to be transported into cells via MCT1, but its clinical usefulness has been hampered by difficulties in delivering the drug systemically.
evidence: Supported by references to Birsoy et al., 2013 and experimental data showing MCT1 knockout cells are resistant to 3BP.

claim: ME3BP-7 is effective against a variety of PDAC cells in vitro.
source: We describe here a novel microencapsulated formulation of 3BP (ME3BP-7), which is effective against a variety of PDAC cells in vitro and remains stable in serum.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell viability assays showing IC50s ranging from 24 to 40 µM in five PDAC cell lines.

claim: ME3BP-7 remains stable in serum.
source: We describe here a novel microencapsulated formulation of 3BP (ME3BP-7), which is effective against a variety of PDAC cells in vitro and remains stable in serum.
evidence: Serum stability assays showing ME3BP-7 retained >70% activity after 8 hr incubation with serum, while free 3BP lost 90% activity by 30 min.

claim: Systemically administered ME3BP-7 significantly reduces pancreatic cancer growth in multiple orthotopic models of pancreatic cancer.
source: Furthermore, systemically administered ME3BP-7 significantly reduces pancreatic cancer growth and metastatic spread in multiple orthotopic models of pancreatic cancer with manageable toxicity.
evidence: Demonstrated in Panc 02.13, TM01212, and TM01098 orthotopic xenograft models with statistical significance (p<0.01).

claim: Systemically administered ME3BP-7 significantly reduces metastatic spread in multiple orthotopic models of pancreatic cancer.
source: Furthermore, systemically administered ME3BP-7 significantly reduces pancreatic cancer growth and metastatic spread in multiple orthotopic models of pancreatic cancer with manageable toxicity.
evidence: Only 3/7 mice treated with ME3BP-7 had any distant metastases compared to all control animals, with significantly decreased number and size (p<0.01).

claim: ME3BP-7 has manageable toxicity in vivo.
source: Furthermore, systemically administered ME3BP-7 significantly reduces pancreatic cancer growth and metastatic spread in multiple orthotopic models of pancreatic cancer with manageable toxicity.
evidence: No overt toxicity was evident after 5 weeks of treatment with ME3BP-7 at 33 mg/kg, and histological evaluation revealed no pathological changes of significance.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma confers a dismal 5-year survival.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) confers a dismal 5-year survival (Sant et al., 2009; Jemal et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sant et al., 2009 and Jemal et al., 2009.

claim: Only a minority of PDAC patients achieve long-term survival even after aggressive multimodal treatment.
source: Even after aggressive multimodal treatment, only a minority of patients achieve long-term survival.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge about PDAC outcomes.

claim: The mainstay of PDAC treatment remains combinations of fluorouracil, irinotecan, oxaliplatin (FOLFIRINOX), or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel.
source: The mainstay of treatment remains combinations of fluorouracil, irinotecan, oxaliplatin (FOLFIRINOX), or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel, which cause severe side effects and offer only modest improvements in survival (Conroy et al., 2011; Conroy et al., 2018; Von Hoff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trials (Conroy et al., 2011; Conroy et al., 2018; Von Hoff et al., 2013).

claim: FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel cause severe side effects and offer only modest improvements in survival.
source: The mainstay of treatment remains combinations of fluorouracil, irinotecan, oxaliplatin (FOLFIRINOX), or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel, which cause severe side effects and offer only modest improvements in survival (Conroy et al., 2011; Conroy et al., 2018; Von Hoff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trials.

claim: Metabolic reprogramming is one of the hallmarks of PDACs.
source: Metabolic reprogramming is one of the hallmarks of PDACs.
evidence: Based on established cancer biology knowledge.

claim: Members of the monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) family are major effectors underlying the aberrant metabolic re-wiring in cancer.
source: Major effectors underlying the aberrant metabolic re-wiring in cancer are members of the monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) family.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about cancer metabolism.

claim: MCT transmembrane proteins mediate the transport of pyruvate, lactate, short-chain fatty acids, and ketones in and out of cells.
source: These transmembrane proteins mediate the transport of pyruvate, lactate, short-chain fatty acids, and ketones in and out of cells (Halestrap and Meredith, 2004; Halestrap, 2012; Halestrap and Wilson, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Halestrap and colleagues.

claim: Increased MCT1 expression in various cancers has been associated with chemoresistance and poor prognosis.
source: Several studies have associated increased monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) expression in various cancers with chemoresistance and poor prognosis (Sant et al., 2009; Leu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2019a; Simões-Sousa et al., 2016; Pinheiro et al., 2008; Miranda-Gonçalves et al., 2021; Latif et al., 2017; Sandforth et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The small molecule MCT1 inhibitor AZD3965 was not found to be effective in the treatment of solid tumors.
source: Although MCT1 is an intriguing biological target, the small molecule MCT1 inhibitor AZD3965 was not found to be effective in the treatment of solid tumors (Beloueche-Babari et al., 2020; Benyahia et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trial results.

claim: 3-Bromopyruvate (3BP) is a potent cytotoxic analog of pyruvic acid with a unique mode of action.
source: 3-Bromopyruvate (3BP) is a potent cytotoxic analog of pyruvic acid with a unique mode of action (Darabedian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Darabedian et al., 2018.

claim: The anticancer effects of 3BP were initially attributed to inhibition of glycolysis.
source: The anticancer effects of 3BP were initially attributed to inhibition of glycolysis (Ganapathy-Kanniappan et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2012; Cardaci et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to earlier studies.

claim: Recent studies have revealed 3BP as an alkylating agent of multiple intracellular proteins.
source: However, recent studies have revealed 3BP as an alkylating agent of multiple intracellular proteins (Darabedian et al., 2018; Ko et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Darabedian et al., 2018 and Ko et al., 2001.

claim: MCT1 expression is essential for the activity of 3BP.
source: MCT1 expression is essential for the activity of 3BP (Birsoy et al., 2013), although effective methods to systemically deliver 3BP have been a major research challenge.
evidence: Supported by citation to Birsoy et al., 2013 and experimental data showing MCT1 KO cells are resistant to 3BP.

claim: Clinical development of 3BP has been hampered by its poor serum stability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, and excessive in vivo toxicity.
source: Clinical development of 3BP has been hampered by its poor serum stability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, and excessive in vivo toxicity despite substantial preclinical and clinical efforts (Azevedo-Silva et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Azevedo-Silva et al., 2016 and Chang et al., 2007.

claim: 3BP alkylates free sulfhydryl groups in plasma proteins, including albumin, resulting in drug inactivation.
source: The biochemical basis for these poor pharmacokinetic features is that 3BP alkylates free sulfhydryl groups in plasma proteins, including albumin, resulting in drug inactivation (Darabedian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Darabedian et al., 2018.

claim: Microencapsulation of 3BP reduces its toxicity.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that microencapsulation of 3BP reduces its toxicity (Chapiro et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Chapiro et al., 2014.

claim: ~20–25% of PDACs exhibit increased expression of SLC16A1 based on comparison of RNAseq datasets from TCGA and CCLE with GTEx portal.
source: Comparison of RNAseq datasets from TCGA and the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) with The Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) portal revealed that ~20–25% of PDACs exhibit increased expression of SLC16A1, the gene encoding MCT1, a mediator of 3BP activity.
evidence: Based on analysis of public genomic databases.

claim: Five PDAC cell lines (MIA PaCa-2, PSN-1, Panc 02.13, AsPC-1, and BxPC-3) were sensitive to 3BP, with IC50s ranging from 24 to 40 µM.
source: Five of the cell lines, MIA PaCa-2, PSN-1, Panc 02.13, AsPC-1, and BxPC-3, were sensitive to 3BP, with IC50s ranging from 24 to 40 µM (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell viability assays with real-time quantitative live-cell imaging.

claim: CFPAC-1 was highly resistant to 3BP, at concentrations of up to 220 µM.
source: In contrast, CFPAC-1 was highly resistant to 3BP, at concentrations of up to 220 µM.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell viability assays.

claim: The expression of MCT1 was much lower in the 3BP-resistant cell line CFPAC-1 than in the other five cell lines.
source: The expression of MCT1 was much lower in the 3BP-resistant cell line CFPAC-1 than in the other five cell lines.
evidence: RNA expression levels from CCLE database and IHC analyses shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: No clear relationship was found between 3BP resistance and the expression of GLUT1 or MCT4 transporters.
source: However, no clear relationship was found between 3BP resistance and the expression of the other transporters.
evidence: Based on analysis of RNA expression levels of SLC2A1 (GLUT1) and SLC16A3 (MCT4) in relation to 3BP sensitivity.

claim: MCT1 protein expression on the cell surface paralleled RNA levels in PDAC cell lines.
source: MCT1 immunohistochemical (IHC) analyses furthermore demonstrated that the expression of the MCT1 protein on the cell surface paralleled RNA levels in these cell lines (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Genetic inactivation of MCT1 in MIA PaCa-2 cells confers resistance to 3BP.
source: In the presence of 50 µM 3BP, the parental cells (Figure 2G), were almost completely eliminated (IC50 24 uM) while the KO cells continued to proliferate (Figure 2F and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-culture experiments with MCT1 WT and KO cells exposed to 3BP.

claim: MCT1 KO cells grew at a rate indistinguishable from the parental cells under normal culture conditions.
source: KO cells grew at a rate indistinguishable from the parental cells under normal culture conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse imaging of cell growth.

claim: Succinyl-substituted cyclodextrins were capable of protecting 3BP in sera more efficiently than hydroxypropyl-substituted versions.
source: Among the β-cyclodextrin formulations tested, we found that succinyl-substituted cyclodextrins were capable of protecting 3BP in sera more efficiently than hydroxypropyl-substituted versions.
evidence: Demonstrated by serum stability assays measuring residual cytotoxicity after serum exposure.

claim: A succinyl-substituted cyclodextrin with an average of 3.4 succinyl groups per cyclodextrin, at a molar ratio of 1.2 β-cyclodextrin per 3BP, performed best.
source: Moreover, a succinyl-substituted cyclodextrin with an average of 3.4 succinyl groups per cyclodextrin, at a molar ratio of 1.2 β-cyclodextrin per 3BP, performed best (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography and serum stability assays.

claim: Free 3BP lost 90% of its activity by 30 min of exposure to serum.
source: Although free 3BP lost 90% of its activity by 30 min of exposure to serum, ME3BP-7 lost <10% of its activity in 30 min (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by serum stability assays using DLD-1 cells.

claim: ME3BP-7 lost <10% of its activity after 30 min of exposure to serum.
source: Although free 3BP lost 90% of its activity by 30 min of exposure to serum, ME3BP-7 lost <10% of its activity in 30 min (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by serum stability assays using DLD-1 cells.

claim: ME3BP-7 retained >70% of its activity after 8 hr of incubation with serum.
source: Remarkably, even after 8 hr of incubation with serum, ME3BP-7 retained >70% of its activity (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by serum stability assays using DLD-1 cells.

claim: Hydroxypropyl-substituted cyclodextrin-3BP complexes lost just over 50% of activity after 30 min of exposure to serum.
source: Hydroxypropyl-substituted cyclodextrin-3BP complexes were more stable than free 3BP, losing just over 50% of its activity after 30 min of exposure to serum.
evidence: Demonstrated by serum stability assays.

claim: Parental MIA PaCa-2 (MCT1 WT) cells were sensitive to ME3BP-7 while MCT1 KO cells were not.
source: Finally, parental MIA PaCa-2 (MCT1 WT) in contrast to MCT1 KO cells were sensitive to the encapsulation of 3BP within ME3BP-7, indicating that the compound retained specificity as well as cytotoxicity for cells expressing MCT1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell viability assays comparing WT and KO cells.

claim: Exposure to either 3BP or ME3BP-7 for as little as 30 min led to the loss of the majority of WT MIA PaCa-2 cells.
source: Exposure to either 3BP or ME3BP-7 for as little as 30 min led to the loss of the majority of WT MIA PaCa-2 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by washout experiments on co-cultures of WT and KO cells.

claim: KO MIA PaCa-2 cells continued to proliferate under all concentrations of 3BP and ME3BP-7 and time points tested.
source: In contrast, KO MIA PaCa-2 cells continued to proliferate under all concentrations of the drugs and time points tested (Figure 4A–D, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by washout experiments with time-lapse imaging.

claim: Gemcitabine and FOLFIRINOX agents exhibited no differential effect on WT and KO cells.
source: In addition, gemcitabine or any of the FOLFIRINOX agents, including irinotecan, oxaliplatin (Video 3), and 5-FU, exhibited no differential effect on WT and KO cells, thus emphasizing the specificity of 3BP and ME3BP-7 for MCT1-expressing cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by washout experiments comparing multiple chemotherapy agents.

claim: 3BP and ME3BP-7 caused cell death of MIA PaCa-2 cells, while the standard of care agents only decreased their proliferation.
source: Moreover, 3BP and ME3BP-7 caused cell death of MIA PaCa-2 cells, while the standard of care agents only decreased their proliferation (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing effects of different drugs on cell viability over time.

claim: Two-thirds of mice in the free 3BP group became ill and died after only two doses at 33 mg/kg.
source: In preliminary experiments, two-thirds of mice in the free 3BP group became ill, showing irrecoverable weight loss, pallor, and decreased activity, and died after only two doses.
evidence: Observed in toxicity studies comparing free 3BP and ME3BP-7.

claim: No overt toxicity was evident even after 5 weeks of treatment with ME3BP-7 at 33 mg/kg.
source: No overt toxicity was evident even after 5 weeks of treatment with ME3BP-7 at the same dose (33 mg/kg) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Observed in toxicity studies in athymic nude mice.

claim: Over the course of 4 weeks of ME3BP-7 treatment, no discernible adverse effects or weight loss was observed in the treated animals in the Panc 02.13 model.
source: Over the course of 4 weeks of treatment (dosed Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays), no discernible adverse effects or weight loss was observed in the treated animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Observed in orthotopic Panc 02.13 xenograft study.

claim: Animals in both ME3BP-7 treatment cohorts showed near-complete abrogation of tumor growth in the Panc 02.13 model (p<0.01).
source: Animals in both treatment cohorts showed near-complete abrogation of tumor growth (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA, Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by bioluminescence imaging over 4 weeks of treatment.

claim: The weight of residual tumors after 4 weeks of ME3BP-7 was significantly decreased in treated animals relative to controls in the Panc 02.13 model (p=0.01).
source: Finally, the weight of residual tumors after 4 weeks of ME3BP-7 was significantly decreased in treated animals relative to controls (p=0.01, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 5D).
evidence: Measured by weighing tumors at necropsy.

claim: Orthotopic TM01212 xenografts expressed moderately high levels of both MCT1 RNA (37 transcripts per million) and protein.
source: Orthotopic TM0212 xenografts expressed moderately high levels of both MCT1 RNA (37 transcripts per million) and protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA expression data and immunohistochemistry.

claim: All control animals in the TM01212 model developed metastases to the lung and liver.
source: More importantly, all control animals developed metastases to the lung and liver, mimicking the behavior of human PDACs (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Observed at necropsy and confirmed by histology.

claim: Only 3/7 mice treated with ME3BP-7 had any distant metastases in the TM01212 model.
source: However, only 3/7 mice treated with ME3BP-7 had any distant metastases, and the number and size of metastases in the treated vs. untreated mice were significantly decreased in treated animals relative to controls (p<0.01, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 6H).
evidence: Observed at necropsy and quantified.

claim: The number and size of metastases were significantly decreased in ME3BP-7 treated animals relative to controls in the TM01212 model (p<0.01).
source: However, only 3/7 mice treated with ME3BP-7 had any distant metastases, and the number and size of metastases in the treated vs. untreated mice were significantly decreased in treated animals relative to controls (p<0.01, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 6H).
evidence: Quantified at necropsy.

claim: Histological evaluation of major organs did not reveal any pathological changes of significance as a result of potential toxicity in ME3BP-7 treated mice.
source: Again, histological evaluation of major organs did not reveal any pathological changes of significance as a result of potential toxicity in the treated mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by histopathological examination of organs.

claim: TM01098 tumor cells expressed high levels of MCT1 RNA (96 transcripts per million) but protein expression exhibited focal staining.
source: Although these tumor cells expressed high levels of MCT1 RNA (96 transcripts per million), protein expression exhibited focal staining (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), which was in contrast to the uniform expression in Panc 02.13 (Figure 1C) and TM01212 xenografts (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA expression data and immunohistochemistry.

claim: Despite focal MCT1 protein expression, significantly slower growth of TM01098 xenografts occurred in animals treated with ME3BP-7 compared to controls based on ultrasound (p<0.01).
source: Despite focal MCT1 protein expression, significantly slower growth of TM01098 xenografts occurred in animals treated with ME3BP-7 compared to controls, based on ultrasound (US) (p<0.01, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D) and tumor weight (p=0.0028, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by ultrasound measurements over time.

claim: Tumor weight was significantly reduced in ME3BP-7 treated TM01098 xenografts compared to controls (p=0.0028).
source: Despite focal MCT1 protein expression, significantly slower growth of TM01098 xenografts occurred in animals treated with ME3BP-7 compared to controls, based on ultrasound (US) (p<0.01, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D) and tumor weight (p=0.0028, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Measured by weighing tumors at necropsy.

claim: 56% (n = 53) of 95 PDAC samples analyzed were positive for MCT1 by immunohistochemistry.
source: Of the 95 samples analyzed, 56% (n = 53) were positive for MCT1 and 44% (n = 42) were negative.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry on tissue microarrays.

claim: Of the 53 MCT1 positive pancreatic cancer tissues, 58% (n = 31) showed low intensity staining, 30% (n = 16) showed intermediate intensity, and 12% (n = 6) showed high intensity.
source: The staining intensity of the 53 MCT1 positive pancreatic cancer tissues was scored as follows: 58% (n = 31), low intensity; 30% (n = 16), intermediate intensity; and 12% (n = 6) high intensity (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: Scored by independent reviewers on tissue microarrays.

claim: None of the 51 normal tissues recorded in the GTEx database expressed average levels of SLC16A1 RNA greater than ~50 transcripts per million.
source: None of the 51 normal tissues recorded in the GTEx database (https://gtexportal.org/home/gene/SLC16A1) expressed average levels of SLC16A1 RNA greater than the approximate threshold required for sensitivity to 3BP in cancer cell lines (~50 transcripts per million, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on analysis of GTEx database.

claim: The highest SLC16A1 expression levels in normal tissues were found in the colon, testis, and uterus (median 37, 38, and 32 transcripts per million, respectively).
source: The highest expression levels in normal tissues were found in the colon, testis, and uterus (median 37, 38, and 32 transcripts per million, respectively, among 142–376 tissue samples assessed for each tissue type) (Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on analysis of GTEx database and citation to Uhlén et al., 2015.

claim: MCT1 RNA levels were consistent with immunohistochemistry; staining was low or absent in normal pancreas, brain, or ovary while readily observed in testis, colon, and uterine tissue.
source: The RNA levels were consistent with the immunohistochemistry; staining was low or absent in normal pancreas, brain, or ovary while readily observed in testis, colon, and uterine tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry on normal tissues.

claim: No discernible damage was found in the colon or uterus of ME3BP-7-treated mice after 4 weeks of treatment, while the pancreatic cancers showed extensive necrosis.
source: On the basis of this information, we carefully examined ME3BP-7-treated mice at necropsy and found no discernible damage after 4 weeks of treatment in either the colon or uterus, while the pancreatic cancers showed extensive necrosis (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Observed by histopathological examination at necropsy.

claim: Pancreatic cancer is predicted to be the third leading cancer killer in the next decade.
source: Pancreatic cancer is a major cause of cancer morbidity and mortality and is predicted to be the third leading cancer killer in the next decade.
evidence: Based on epidemiological projections.

claim: Average life expectancy in advanced pancreatic cancer is under a year.
source: Average life expectancy is under a year in advanced disease, and there is an undeniable unmet need for better therapeutics.
evidence: Based on clinical knowledge of pancreatic cancer outcomes.

claim: A sizable fraction of pancreatic cancers express relatively high levels of MCT1 while the same is barely detectable in normal pancreas.
source: Public datasets reveal that a sizable fraction of pancreatic cancers express relatively high levels of a membrane protein, MCT1, (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017), while the same is barely detectable in normal pancreas.
evidence: Based on analysis of TCGA data and immunohistochemistry.

claim: Specific small-molecule inhibitors of MCT1 have not shown any benefit in human clinical trials.
source: Despite the promise, specific small-molecule inhibitors of MCT1 have not shown any benefit in human clinical trials, rendering MCT1 an unrealized but exciting biological target.
evidence: Based on clinical trial results with AZD3965.

claim: ME3BP-7 differs from antibody-drug conjugates in that it is a small molecule.
source: ME3BP-7 differs from antibody-drug conjugates in several important respects. First, ME3BP-7 is a small molecule, drastically reducing drug production challenges and cost.
evidence: Based on comparison of molecular properties.

claim: ME3BP-7 itself mediates the targeting as well as the toxicity, while antibody-drug conjugates use an antibody for targeting and a separate small molecule to kill cells.
source: Second, ME3BP-7 itself mediates the targeting as well as the toxicity, while antibody-drug conjugates use an antibody for targeting and a separate, small molecule to kill cells (Thomas et al., 2016; Baah et al., 2021; Drago et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on mechanistic understanding of how ME3BP-7 and antibody-drug conjugates work.

claim: MCT1 is overexpressed in subsets of mesotheliomas, leukemias, and several other tumor types.
source: Although we focused on pancreatic cancers in this study, MCT1 is overexpressed in subsets of mesotheliomas, leukemias, and several other tumor types (https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000155380-SLC16A1/pathology).
evidence: Based on data from the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: One important mechanism of resistance to ME3BP-7 is expected to be loss of the target MCT1.
source: As with any targeted agent, we expect one important mechanism of resistance will be loss of the target (Kobayashi et al., 2005; Shah and Fry, 2019; Garrett and Arteaga, 2011).
evidence: Based on general principles of targeted therapy resistance and citations.

claim: MCT1 is not an oncogene, so loss of MCT1 is conceivable as a resistance mechanism.
source: MCT1 is not an oncogene, so loss of MCT1 is conceivable.
evidence: Based on understanding of MCT1 function and oncogene biology.

claim: ME3BP-7 is uniquely fast-acting compared to other drugs now used in the clinic to treat patients with pancreatic cancer.
source: The results in Figure 3 show that ME3BP-7 is uniquely fast-acting compared to other drugs now used in the clinic to treat patients with pancreatic cancer.
evidence: Demonstrated by washout experiments showing cell death after 30 min exposure.

claim: Despite striking effects in vitro, ME3BP-7 did not induce true regressions of extant tumors in mice, though growth was slowed and metastases were markedly reduced.
source: On the other hand, a limitation of our study is that, despite these striking effects in vitro, we were not able to induce true regressions of extant tumors in mice, though growth was slowed (Figures 5 and 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and metastases were markedly reduced (Figure 6H).
evidence: Based on in vivo tumor growth and metastasis data.

claim: Different methods for administering ME3BP-7 may improve its in vivo potency.
source: We speculate that different methods for administering ME3BP-7 may improve its in vivo potency.
evidence: Based on speculation about improving drug delivery.

claim: The combination of irinotecan or liposomal irinotecan with ME3BP-7 could improve the potency as well as address the pockets of heterogeneity with low MCT1 in pancreatic cancer.
source: Our data suggests that the combination of irinotecan, or liposomal irinotecan as described in the NAPOLI-3 trial (Wang-Gillam et al., 2019; Wainberg et al., 2023), with ME3BP-7 could improve the potency as well as address the pockets of heterogeneity with low MCT1 in pancreatic cancer (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on data showing different mechanisms of action and speculation about combination therapy.

claim: ME3BP-7 could alleviate the resistance to glutaminase inhibition, leading to an efficacious combination.
source: Similarly, ME3BP-7 could alleviate the resistance to glutaminase inhibition, leading to an efficacious combination (Ammar et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on citation and speculation about combination therapy.

claim: Severe extracellular acidity around solid tumors due to MCT1 overexpression causes immune exclusion.
source: Finally, severe extracellular acidity around solid tumors, due to MCT1 overexpression causing immune exclusion (Feng et al., 2024), suggests a combination of immune checkpoint inhibitors with ME3BP-7 could improve therapeutic outcomes.
evidence: Based on citation to Feng et al., 2024.

claim: A combination of immune checkpoint inhibitors with ME3BP-7 could improve therapeutic outcomes.
source: Finally, severe extracellular acidity around solid tumors, due to MCT1 overexpression causing immune exclusion (Feng et al., 2024), suggests a combination of immune checkpoint inhibitors with ME3BP-7 could improve therapeutic outcomes.
evidence: Based on speculation about combination therapy.

claim: Clinical trials will be the only way to reliably determine whether ME3BP-7 could serve as an adjuvant therapy for patients with pancreatic cancers.
source: However, given the limitations of administering the drug to small animals, we believe that clinical trials will be the only way to reliably determine whether ME3BP-7 could serve as an adjuvant therapy for patients with pancreatic cancers.
evidence: Based on limitations of preclinical models and inference about need for clinical testing.

claim: ME3BP-7 shows efficacy across multiple pancreatic cancer model systems.
source: Our results highlight that ME3BP-7 shows efficacy across multiple pancreatic cancer model systems and potentially represents a powerful new therapeutic agent for this cancer type and perhaps others that express the drug's target protein.
evidence: Demonstrated in Panc 02.13, TM01212, and TM01098 models.

claim: ME3BP-7 potentially represents a powerful new therapeutic agent for pancreatic cancer and perhaps others that express MCT1.
source: Our results highlight that ME3BP-7 shows efficacy across multiple pancreatic cancer model systems and potentially represents a powerful new therapeutic agent for this cancer type and perhaps others that express the drug's target protein.
evidence: Based on preclinical efficacy data and knowledge of MCT1 expression in other cancers.
